Debt crisis eases for Mexican transport and logistics firms as credit lines restored

MEXICO CITY, June 13—A severe debt crisis that gripped Mexico’s transportation and logistics industry has been resolved following emergency negotiations with lenders, industry officials said Thursday. The crisis, triggered by a sudden freeze in short-term credit last month, forced several major carriers and rail operators to halt or curtail services amid mounting unpaid obligations.

Among the affected companies was Ferrocarril Mexicano SA de CV, which temporarily suspended select freight operations as it struggled to meet debt repayments. “The liquidity crunch was unprecedented,” said company spokesperson Luis Herrera. “We are relieved that agreements reached with creditors over the weekend have allowed us to resume normal operations.”

The crisis erupted after a series of loan defaults by smaller firms led banks to tighten lending criteria across the sector. Credit lines vital for daily fuel purchases and payroll were withdrawn, leading to a cascade of missed payments and operational cutbacks. According to the Mexican Transporters Association, at least 22 medium and large logistics firms faced acute cash-flow shortages in late May.

“The disruption was felt nationwide, with cargo movement dropping nearly 30% in the first week of June,” said association president Marisol Ortega. “The swift restoration of credit facilities has been crucial in stabilizing the sector.”

Unions representing rail and trucking workers welcomed the resolution but warned that vulnerabilities remain. “We urge companies and banks to strengthen risk controls so this doesn’t happen again,” said union leader Rafael Gómez.

Industry analysts estimate that while full recovery may take several weeks, most suspended routes have resumed service as of Wednesday.
